mandate: Pilot-approved bracket 4 (bracket_report.json: floor 4 on four Game Changers — Enlightened Tutor, Smothering Tithe, Teferi's Protection, Worldly Tutor — target 4, within_target true). The pilot's own standing brief is power, consistency and menace (data/decks/ur-dragon/pilot_feedback.md); after the first logged game they narrowed it: 'The bottleneck is mana consistency, not card selection' (log.jsonl 001).
archetype: Five-colour Dragon typal ramp-midrange: buy the curve down with eminence and four printed reducers, land fat fliers, and convert with per-Dragon entry triggers or by multiplying one attacking Dragon. Written deliberately without an archetype keyword. deck_audit._ARCHETYPE_HINTS is a keyword read over this string; the previous frame's wording matched the tutors-4-8 / protection-4-6 template and the audit inherited it, which is wrong for a 99 holding 27 creature entries, 24 Dragons, six narrow tutors, one contained line and zero two-card infinites. With no keyword matched the audit falls back to the base targets, which are the right yardstick here (diagnosis.json archetype).

role_assignment.default_role: Engine seat that owns the long game, and must stop pretending it owns the early one. strategy:whos-the-beatdown.metagame-clock: 'four-player games trend long, so inevitability compounds — engines are the default winning plan'; eminence discounts every other Dragon spell from the command zone with nothing to cast and nothing to remove, and the per-Dragon payoffs scale with a board nobody else is building. The measurements force the posture rather than merely permitting it (◆ goldfish, 10,000 iterations, seed 42): mean available mana 4.219 at turn five and 4.669 at six, land drops 0.834 / 0.670 / 0.525 on turns three to five, against 26 maindeck nonland entries at mana value five or more. So turns one to four are fixing and reducers, not threats.
role_assignment.pivot_trigger: The window (strategy:multiplayer.pivot-window) opens on an ENTRY board, not on a loop — the loop is gone with Aggravated Assault. Concretely: a per-Dragon damage payoff already on the battlefield (Dragon Tempest, Terror of the Peaks or Scourge of Valkas) plus one widener (Ancient Gold Dragon, Miirym, Lathliss, Utvara Hellkite, Sarkhan Fireblood), then cast one nontoken Dragon. Two checker-passed, presentable stacks price what such a board does: stack 001 puts 255 damage on offer at X=17 and its final_state reads 'lethality confirmed', killing every opponent on that board; stack 002 deals 64 in 12 separately-targeted instances and kills the 32-life seat. ◆ The declaration measures the two-legged version at 0.240 assembled / 0.153 by turn six, mean turn 4.983 — so this is a window you build toward and often do not get. The doc's bar is 'protection up, table tapped out, interaction counted and accounted for'; the protection component is the deck's second-deepest at 0.764 assembled / 0.655 by turn six, so the bar is usually meetable on the turn the payoff arrives.

gameplan_by_phase.early_t1_t4: Land every drop, take fixing over utility, and treat a reducer as the real acceleration. The turn-three land drop is 0.834 and then falls to 0.670 and 0.525 (◆ goldfish), so a turn-two rock or Farseek is worth more here than in a deck that can afford a miss; ramp-or-fixing is drawn 0.820 assembled / 0.712 by turn six, the deepest component in the deck, while the four-card reducer group is 0.518 / 0.419. Mulligan on strategy:mulligans.engine-hands: 'Payoffs without the enabler are blanks until the engine exists' — and in this deck the enabler class is lands, rocks and the four reducers, not the Dragons. Posture is deflection (strategy:multiplayer.threat-deflection), with the doc's own warning attached: 'combo decks look non-threatening while advancing in secret, which is exactly why experienced tables hit the quiet ramp player'.
gameplan_by_phase.mid_t5_t7: The squeeze, and the deck has to deploy through it. Deploy in waves under strategy:resource-hedging.wrath-math — 'assume the wrath — over a four-player game one is near-certain — so deploy in waves, hold a rebuild package' — which this deck can actually do: Miirym and Lathliss rebuild in tokens, Teferi's Protection and Heroic Intervention cover a whole board, and Eerie Interlude answers a sweeper at instant speed for {2}{W} (engine.json adds it to the declared eight; the declaration still says eight). The commander is NOT the mid-game plan: ◆ mean cast turn 8.172, cast by turn six in 4.1%, and never cast by turn ten in 7,170 of 10,000 iterations. Sneak Attack compresses a finisher into {R} for one turn (✓ stack 005: Drakuseth enters hasty, its attack trigger fires for 4+3+3, connects for 7, all 17 stands after the mandatory end-step sacrifice) — and the same stack refutes Sneak Attack ever reaching the command zone.
gameplan_by_phase.late_t8_plus: ◆ The combat model's clock: kill by turn 8 in 24.4%, by turn 10 in 52.2%, mean kill turn 8.203, no kill inside ten turns in 47.8%. Read it as a clock on ONE unopposed seat at 40, never as a win rate — nothing blocks in that model, which makes the clock optimistic, while five combat effects (Ancient Gold Dragon, Atarka World Render, Hellkite Tyrant, Klauth, Thrakkus the Butcher) and five Treasure sources (Atsushi, Cavern-Hoard Dragon, Goldspan Dragon, Old Gnawbone, Smothering Tithe) are unreadable to the parser, which makes the board a floor. Both directions are stated in goldfish meta.model_assumptions. What the deck is actually doing this late is looking for the entry board, because the two lethal proofs are both entry boards and neither declared kill is verified as reachable.

engines.engine: THE ENTRY KILL's proven instance: one d20 roll turns combat damage into N simultaneous Dragon entries, and every Tempest trigger sees X = the whole board. At the scenario's fixed roll of 15, X = 17 across 15 triggers — 255 available at one target, the 30-life seat dead to the second trigger, and Miirym copies none of the tokens because they are not nontoken.
engines.evidence: verified stack 001 (data/decks/ur-dragon/stacks/001-tempest-gold-dragon-burst.json, checker.verdict pass, presentable); combo_details lists the pair as the deck's only contained line (bracket 3, popularity 24453, produces 'Near-infinite damage')

engines.piece: Miirym, Sentinel Wyrm + Panharmonicon (with Terror of the Peaks and Dragon Tempest)
engines.engine: The trigger multiplier. Panharmonicon doubles every trigger in the cascade because each is caused by a creature entering, so one Lathliss cast becomes two nonlegendary 6/6 copies and 64 damage in 12 separately-targeted instances — 36 from Terror at 6 apiece and 28 from Tempest at X = 4,4,5,5,5,5. The loop is finite by construction: every later entry is a token and both 'nontoken' clauses exclude them.
engines.evidence: verified stack 002 (data/decks/ur-dragon/stacks/002-miirym-panharmonicon-doubling.json, checker.verdict pass, presentable); kills the 32-life seat, and its own final_state states the 40-life seat survives at 8 — 64 against 72 is the shortfall, stated rather than assumed

engines.piece: Sneak Attack + Drakuseth, Maw of Flames
engines.engine: The cheat lane, and the only checker-passed arrow in the deck that reaches a finisher: {R} puts a 7/7 in with haste, the attack trigger (not a cast trigger) fires for 4+3+3 before blockers, it connects for 7, and all 17 damage stands after the mandatory end-step sacrifice. Its limit is proven in the same artifact — Sneak Attack cannot touch the command zone, so it is not a route to the nine-mana commander.

engines.piece: Eminence + Urza's Incubator, Herald's Horn, Dragonspeaker Shaman, Dragonlord's Servant
engines.engine: Ignition, and it is what this deck has instead of ramp at the top end: eminence works from the command zone with nothing to cast and nothing an opponent can remove, and four printed reducers stack on it. An oracle scan of all 95 entries for cost reduction returns exactly those four plus eminence and Cavern-Hoard Dragon's self-reduction (engine.json ignition stage).
engines.evidence: oracle text (cards.json) + ◆ goldfish 'Cost reducer drawn' 0.518 assembled / 0.419 by turn six, mean turn 3.28; crossed with ramp the turn-5-commander hand is 0.417 / 0.285. At four cards deck-audit prices it at 0.258 in an opening seven.

engines.piece: Treasure fuel: Atsushi, Cavern-Hoard Dragon, Goldspan Dragon, Old Gnawbone, Rapacious Dragon, Smothering Tithe (and Smaug the Magnificent, whose hoard is its own trigger's input)
engines.engine: The one-expensive-turn subsidy. A Treasure is a one-shot stockpile spent only when lands and rocks fall short, so it does not raise the average — mean available mana is 4.219 at turn five with the model on and off alike — it buys the single turn a nine-mana commander needs. Turning the model on took commander-by-turn-six from 0.0% to 4.1%.
engines.evidence: ◆ goldfish with model_treasures on, 10,000 iterations: 'A Treasure source drawn' 0.732 assembled / 0.618 by turn six. Every Treasure-derived MANA figure is a FLOOR: five of the sources are named in meta.treasure_sources_not_modelled.

engines.piece: Protection held for the big turn: Teferi's Protection, Heroic Intervention, Flawless Maneuver, Boros Charm, Deflecting Swat, Counterspell, Swan Song, Dovin's Veto (+ Eerie Interlude)
engines.engine: Insurance on the pivot turn rather than on the commander — which is the correct target here, because the commander is not the plan. Two of the nine are conditionally free: Flawless Maneuver and Deflecting Swat read 'If you control a commander', and this commander is usually in the command zone (engine.json protection stage).
engines.evidence: ◆ goldfish 'Protection held for the big turn' 0.764 assembled / 0.655 by turn six, mean turn 2.796 — the deck's second-deepest component after ramp

engines.engine: The only card in the 99 that puts a commander onto the battlefield from the command zone — an oracle scan of all 95 entries returns it and the commander itself. It is therefore the deck's only route to its largest payoff that beats turn eight, and none of it is checked: whether the ETB reaches the command zone, whether the granted haste makes an attack legal, and whether the end-step return adds to the tax under CR 903.8 are all open.
engines.evidence: oracle text (cards.json) + engine.json conversion stage; NO stack covers it — see candidate_missing_lines

key_tensions: TWO KILLS, AND THE SCHEMA CANNOT ADD THEM UP. THE ENTRY KILL measures 0.240 assembled / 0.153 by turn six; THE COMBAT KILL measures 0.204 / 0.128. Both carry UNVERIFIED in their own declared titles. They are 3.6 points apart, which is the finding — not which is nominally ahead — and they must never be summed or averaged, because a goldfish target is an assembly rate for one named set of cards and there is no expression in the declaration for the union of two plans. What breaks the tie is evidence, not rate: two presentable checker-passed stacks (001, 002) are entry boards and NO passing stack names any combat-kill multiplier at all.

THE PROOF IS LETHALITY; THE GAP IS REACHABILITY. Stack 001 kills every opponent on its board and stack 002 kills a 32-life seat — those are facts about boards, not about frequencies. 001's own reachability is better than it reads: with N tokens, X is N+2 across N triggers with targets locked at stacking time, so three seats at 40 needs 3·⌈40/(N+2)⌉ ≤ N — N=12 holds and N=11 fails, which is a d20 at 12 or better: nine faces of twenty, 45% (engine.json open_questions, derived). That is arithmetic on the printed card, ◆ at best, and the board it starts from still grants the payoff, the widener and a connection.

THE COMMANDER IS THE NAME OF THE DECK AND NOT ITS PLAN. ◆ mean cast turn 8.172, by turn six 4.1%, never inside ten turns in 7,170 of 10,000. strategy:deckbuilding.archetype-selection's distinction is the one that binds: 'built around your commander is not reliant on it'. This list is correctly built — 24 Dragons that want eminence's discount whether or not the nine-mana body ever lands — and the risk is the pilot playing it as though the commander were the payoff.

MANA IS THE BINDING AXIS AND THE HEADLINE COLOUR FIGURE IS A DECOY. 31 land copies against strategy:deckbuilding.ratios' '36–38 lands, 10–12 ramp, 10 card draw, 10–12 targeted removal, 3–4 board wipes', and 43 sources against Burgess's 31 + 5 colours + a mana value 9 commander = 45. But deck-audit's alarming −15 colour-sources figure is BLACK, and exactly three cards in the 99 want black (diagnosis.json colour-sources axis). Red is the colour that matters: 53.9% of the pip load on 30.0% of the sources, on-curve 0.515 from lands alone.

FOURTEEN OF THIRTY-ONE LANDS ENTER TAPPED (45%), FIVE ALWAYS. strategy:deckbuilding.mana-base: 'Duke treats entering tapped as a real drawback — around eight taplands is comfortable in a slow deck, near zero in an aggressive one'; strategy:deckbuilding.mana-base.color-sources adds that Karsten caps pure taplands at about four. This deck is slow, so the eight-tapland reading is the right one and it is still nearly double. The goldfish cannot see this at all — it models one land drop per turn and no tapped state — so the tempo cost is real and unmeasured, which is exactly what the pilot asked to have audited (log.jsonl 001).

candidate_missing_lines.title: THE ENTRY KILL at a board you can actually reach: a payoff, a widener, and one nontoken Dragon cast into three seats at 40
candidate_missing_lines.why_plausible: Stacks 001 and 002 both pass and both kill, but 001 starts from a connected Ancient Gold Dragon with the roll fixed at 15 and 002 states its own shortfall (64 against 72). The declaration prices the two-legged version at 0.240 assembled / 0.153 by turn six, and after today's correction the damage leg is three cards. What nobody has resolved is whether a REACHABLE version reaches three opponents at 40, or what the exact shortfall is. This is the deck's central open question.

candidate_missing_lines.title: Hellkite Courser: does its ETB put The Ur-Dragon onto the battlefield, does the granted haste make an attack legal, and does the end-step return add to the tax under CR 903.8?
candidate_missing_lines.why_plausible: An oracle scan of all 95 entries returns Hellkite Courser as the only card that puts a commander onto the battlefield from the command zone, and stack 005 already refutes the obvious alternative (Sneak Attack cannot). With the commander never cast inside ten turns in 7,170 of 10,000 iterations, this is the only route to the deck's largest payoff that beats turn eight — and every part of it is unchecked.

candidate_missing_lines.title: The Ur-Dragon's attack trigger: one card per attacking Dragon, and may the permanent it puts from hand be any permanent?
candidate_missing_lines.why_plausible: This is the payoff the Courser question exists to reach. It is a triggered-ability reading of the commander's own printed text and no artifact in the deck covers it; every claim about what the commander does once it lands currently rests on a paraphrase.

candidate_missing_lines.title: THE COMBAT KILL's shape: Thrakkus the Butcher doubling Moltensteel Dragon, and the order of pump against doubling
candidate_missing_lines.why_plausible: The declared kill measures 0.204 assembled / 0.128 by turn six on a two-card multiplier leg, and no passing stack — presentable or withheld — names Atarka, Thrakkus, Radiant Destiny or Garruk's Uprising (diagnosis.json lean_into, grepped across all six files). Thrakkus doubles power on attack and Moltensteel pumps itself for life, so the answer depends on ordering, which is a rules question nobody has asked. Until it is asked, the whole second plan is prose.

candidate_missing_lines.title: Atarka, World Render on Drakuseth: double strike doubles the combat damage and does NOT fire the attack trigger twice
candidate_missing_lines.why_plausible: engine.json states the narrow version deliberately, because the obvious version is wrong: the attack trigger fires once on declare. Stack 005 already establishes Drakuseth's 4+3+3 and its 7 in the air on a hasty turn, so the increment Atarka actually buys is checkable and unchecked — and it is the other half of the multiplier leg above.

candidate_missing_lines.title: Smaug the Magnificent's attack trigger cannot be fed by Old Gnawbone within one combat
candidate_missing_lines.why_plausible: engine.json argues from printed timing: Smaug's trigger goes on the stack in declare-attackers and counts Treasures when it resolves, before the combat damage step, which is when Gnawbone's 'deals combat damage to a player' clause makes any. If that is right the pairing is a two-combat arrow, not a one-combat one, and the pilot should sequence accordingly — but it is a timing claim, not a checked one.

candidate_missing_lines.title: Moltensteel Dragon as a lone clock: sixteen life for twelve damage, as it actually happened
candidate_missing_lines.why_plausible: log_annotations 001 records the play from the first logged game and flags it unproven: the pilot paid sixteen life to hit for twelve while locked out of three colours. The arithmetic is consistent with the printed card ({R/P}: +1/+0), but no stack artifact covers the phyrexian-mana payment, and this is the deck's floor-case threat — what it does when nothing else is castable.

matchup_frames.vs_sweeper_control: You are the inevitability seat and they are trying to be (strategy:whos-the-beatdown.metagame-clock). Play strategy:resource-hedging.wrath-math straight: 'assume the wrath — over a four-player game one is near-certain — so deploy in waves, hold a rebuild package'. This deck is unusually well set up for it and unusually punished by ignoring it: 0.764 assembled protection means the answer is usually there, and Teferi's Protection, Heroic Intervention and Eerie Interlude each cover the whole board rather than one permanent, while Miirym and Lathliss rebuild in tokens. The specific error to avoid is jamming the payoff before the widener: the entry board is worth almost nothing without both legs, so a Dragon Tempest resolved into open blue mana on turn five buys a counterspell for their best turn, not yours. Sequence the scariest piece last (strategy:multiplayer.pivot-window).
matchup_frames.vs_stax: Role flips: strategy:threat-assessment.resource-denial says 'you rarely own the long game under an assembling lock, so you are the beatdown, racing the lock's completion'. Taxes hit this deck exactly where it is thinnest — 26 maindeck nonland entries at mana value five or more on 4.219 mean mana at turn five — so name the piece that beats YOU rather than the scariest piece, and note that only three of the interactive cards are counterspells and a counter answers a lock piece only on the way in. Two things break a tax: eminence discounts every Dragon spell from the command zone whether or not the commander is castable, and a Treasure burst converts one good turn into the one expensive cast. ONE DIRECTION IS CLOSED BY THE PILOT: log.jsonl 001 lost to a turn-two-or-three Blood Moon that turned 22 of 31 lands into Mountains, and the pilot's stated decision is that this is an accepted risk at bracket 3+ and they are not building around it. strategy:deckbuilding.power-level.barometers files Blood Moon under mass land denial — 'Armageddon, Ruination, Sunder, Winter Orb, Blood Moon' — which is 'not anywhere in Brackets 1-3'; this frame records that and prescribes nothing against it. What the game IS evidence for is the mana base generally, which the pilot did ask to have audited.
matchup_frames.vs_aggro: The one matchup where 27 creature entries — 25 of them Dragons, counting the commander, so 24 in the 99 — do defensive work for free: fat fliers block, and strategy:multiplayer.asymmetry's warning — '~120 combined life behind three defenses makes incremental combat damage a losing plan' — is the OPPONENT's problem here, not yours. The risk is the reverse of the sweeper matchup: an early attacker makes you spend removal you were holding for the pivot turn, and this deck's removal is 7 damage-based plus 2 spot, so a single big body eats several cards. strategy:threat-assessment.answer-economy is the discipline — the bar is 'ends the game or ends my deck's function', and against a fair aggressive board a chump block from a 5/5 Dragon token is cheaper than a card. Do not race: mean board power is 4.451 at turn five and 6.423 at turn six (◆), which is a defensive board long before it is an offensive one.
matchup_frames.vs_combo: You lose the long game you thought you owned, so the clock reading inverts: their turn-15 picture is better than yours and strategy:whos-the-beatdown.metagame-clock's table test says whoever likes it less should be attacking now. In practice this deck cannot interact its way to a win — 12 interaction copies, of which exactly three answer a spell on the stack — an oracle scan of all 95 entries for 'counter target' returns Counterspell, Swan Song and Dovin's Veto and nothing else — so the plan is to present the entry board early and accept the deflection cost (strategy:multiplayer.threat-deflection). Hold the counterspells for the piece that wins rather than the piece that scales, per strategy:threat-assessment.answer-economy: 'held answers rot — against combo, or lethal already on board, the last profitable moment is now.' Note the asymmetry in the doc's own warning: this deck reads as the quiet ramp player and will be treated as one, which buys turns against the table and none against the player who is also quietly ramping.

distribution_notes: 95 entries / 100 copies (◆ deck-facts). 31 land copies across 26 entries; 69 nonland entries including the commander, so 68 maindeck, of which 26 cost five or more. Curve by mana value: 0:1, 1:5, 2:11, 3:17, 4:8, 5:10, 6:9, 7:5, 8:1, 9:2 — modal at 3 against the format's modal 2, with 24 cards at 5-7 and 3 at 8-9 against the ~1.5 at 8+ that strategy:deckbuilding.curve puts in an average deck. That section's instruction is 'Build to hit 2, 4 and 6 mana reliably', and the goldfish says 4 is where this deck stops doing so: mean available mana 3.674 at turn four, 4.219 at five, 4.669 at six. Lands: 9 basic (4 Mountain, 3 Forest, 1 Island, 1 Plains — no Swamp), 14 of 31 entering tapped (45%), 5 always. Colour, lands only: G 0.810, W 0.592, U 0.592, R 0.515, B 0.217; with rocks and dorks G 0.918, W 0.810, U 0.810, R 0.742, B 0.524. Pip share R 0.539 on source share 0.300 — the one real mismatch. Roles (card_roles covers 96.8%; Chaos Warp, Rishkar's Expertise and Sneak Attack have no pattern): 27 threat:body, 10 value:etb, 9 utility:activated, 8 ramp:rock, 7 ramp:treasure, 7 removal:damage, 7 threat:tokens, 6 tutor:narrow, 5 ramp:cost-reduction, 5 protection:self, 3 counterspell, 3 payoff:typal, 1 removal:sweeper. Five sources produce RESTRICTED mana that cannot pay a coloured activation cost — Desolation of Smaug, Klauth, Maelstrom of the Spirit Dragon, Sarkhan Fireblood, Unclaimed Territory — which is why they accelerate toward the commander without accelerating what it then does; the declaration prices that group at 0.306 assembled.
overall_assessment: This is a linear deck (strategy:critical-mass) that has just lost the non-linear escape hatch it used to have. With Aggravated Assault gone there is no loop and no two-card infinite in the 99 — deck-facts counts one contained line and zero infinites — so the whole plan is the threshold: put a per-Dragon payoff and a widener on the same battlefield and cast one nontoken Dragon. The doc's tradeoff applies exactly: 'linear strategies give up flexibility in exchange for power', and its Commander correction is the sentence to build against — 'the linear deck needs redundancy that shrugs off three answers, or a deflection posture that keeps them unspent'. This list has more of the second than the first: 0.764 assembled protection is real, but the entry kill's damage leg is three cards and its widener leg five, and the whole target assembles 0.240 / 0.153 by turn six. What changed today is the evidence, and it changed in the deck's favour on lethality and against it on frequency. TWO presentable checker-passed stacks now eliminate a player — 001 at 255 available damage with 'lethality confirmed' in its own final_state, 002 at 64 in 12 targeted instances — so the previous reading of this deck as having no proven kill was wrong. Set against that: correcting two mis-declared groups moved the entry kill from 0.481 / 0.356 to 0.240 / 0.153 and the combat kill from 0.411 / 0.290 to 0.204 / 0.128, so the deck's own declaration now says its likelier plan is a one-in-four assembly, and the 3.6-point gap between the two plans is small enough that the tie is broken by evidence rather than rate. And underneath all of it sits the mana, which is what the pilot said after the only game on record and what diagnosis.json's terminal verdict says too: 31 lands against a 36-38 floor, land drops 0.834 / 0.670 / 0.525, 45% of the lands entering tapped, and a commander that arrives in 28.3% of ten-turn games. Above the mana line this deck is in good shape and the pilot is right about it. The honest one-line world-view: this is an inevitability deck whose inevitability is priced at turn eight and whose mana pays for turn five — and the first correction is not another Dragon, it is lands (◆/★, and diagnosis.json carries a TERMINAL skeptic verdict of 'fail' at iteration 3 with two findings undischarged — a miscounted enumeration in cut_candidates[4] and an over-claim in lean_into[2], both text-level rather than arithmetic — so its figures are usable and its recommendations are under review, not settled).
gaps: The basic-land floor for a five-colour deck running Farseek, Nature's Lore and Skyshroud Claim: at what basics count does tutor whiff become material, and how does that trade against generic fixing? strategy:deckbuilding.mana-base budgets SOURCES and strategy:deckbuilding.mana-base.color-sources budgets pips, but neither section says anything about a fetch package whiffing. This is the pilot's own first question from log.jsonl 001 and log_annotations already routes it to research-strategy.

A Commander-specific tapland budget. The doc has Duke's 'around eight taplands is comfortable in a slow deck' and Karsten's cap 'at about four' pure taplands — two numbers that disagree by a factor of two and neither of which is denominated for a 31-to-38-land five-colour deck. This deck is at 14 (5 always), the goldfish cannot see tapped state at all, and the pilot explicitly asked whether it is costing tempo.

How to choose between TWO unconnected win plans by measured assembly rate. strategy:deckbuilding.threat-density has Eisenherz's 'a Plan A and Plan B' and 'Separate ceiling from median: the ceiling build runs one spectacular finisher and loses when it's answered; the median runs three cheap ones and closes from any board' — but nothing on what to do when two plans measure 0.240 and 0.204 and share cards. The doc says cut the least efficient; it does not say how to price 3.6 points of separation, which is the exact decision in front of this deck.

Dice- and coin-based payoffs as probability. strategy:combat-math.probability gives the method — 'count successes in the deck and cards seen, read the cumulative probability' — for library questions, and nothing for a d20 threshold. Stack 001's kill needs a 12 or better (45%) and Ancient Gold Dragon is in the corpus's most-played Dragon shells; a short section on reading a die as a leg of a plan would let the frame stop deriving it inline.

A section on a critical-mass deck whose largest payoff is an uncastable commander. strategy:multiplayer.commander-insurance prices protecting a commander you cast and strategy:deckbuilding.archetype-selection warns that 'built around your commander is not reliant on it', but neither addresses the case measured here: a commander cast in 28.3% of ten-turn games whose static command-zone ability is doing all the work. The right advice may be that this is FINE and the frame currently has to argue it from first principles.
